\chapter{Letters From Home and Money}

\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}

Complete the last lesson of chapter 45: i can write the letter gha and the ai sign, and find each one in a word I already say.

\section[gha]{\gu{ઘ} (gha) — the letter that opens \gu{ઘર}}

\label{lesson:GU-W45-gha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \gu{તે} and \gu{ઠ} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\gu{ઘર}} (\emph{ghar}), \textquotedblleft{}home\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \gu{ઘ}}
\textbf{\gu{ઘ}} — \emph{gha}, a \emph{g} with a puff of breath after it.

It opens \textbf{\gu{ઘર}} (\emph{ghar}), \textquotedblleft{}home\textquotedblright{}. Say \emph{gar}, then \emph{ghar}: the second has the breath.

\subsection*{Writing: \gu{ઘ}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/GU-W45-gha-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \gu{ઘ} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: circle the upper lobe, turn through the middle, and round the lower body
  \item \textbf{2.} lift, then descend the right spine and turn through its lower foot — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: t30apps.com, ‘Gujarati Alphabet Writing Practice’, version 1.0, \gu{ઘ} animation, first and second SVG paths.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\gu{ઘર}} and point at \gu{ઘ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \gu{ઘ} three times, saying \emph{gh} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \gu{ઠ}, then \gu{ઘ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\gu{ઘર}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \gu{ઘ}? (\textbf{gha}, \emph{gh}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\gu{ઘર}}, \emph{ghar}, \textquotedblleft{}home\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai sign]{\gu{ૈ} (ai sign) — the ai sign in \gu{પૈસા}}

\label{lesson:GU-W45-ai-sign}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \gu{ઠ} and \gu{ઘ} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\gu{પૈસા}} (\emph{paisā}), \textquotedblleft{}money\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \gu{ૈ}}
\textbf{\gu{ૈ}} — the \emph{ai} sign.

It sits above \textbf{\gu{પ}} in \textbf{\gu{પૈસા}} (\emph{paisā}), \textquotedblleft{}money\textquotedblright{}. You already write \textbf{\gu{ે}}, one stroke above a consonant, for \emph{e}. Two strokes, \textbf{\gu{ૈ}}, make it \emph{ai}.

\subsection*{Writing: \gu{ૈ}}
Put your pen on \gu{ૈ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start this letter or which way to travel}. It is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\gu{પૈસા}} and point at \gu{ૈ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \gu{ૈ} three times, saying \emph{ai} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \gu{ઘ}, then \gu{ૈ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\gu{પૈસા}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \gu{ૈ}? (\textbf{ai sign}, \emph{ai}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\gu{પૈસા}}, \emph{paisā}, \textquotedblleft{}money\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
